basis: Lincoln to Hamlin 24 Dec 1860 (p.86): 'I need a man of Democratic antecedents from New England. I cannot get a fair share of that element in without.' Lincoln to Kellogg 11 Dec 1860 (p.77): 'Entertain no proposition for a compromise in regard to the extension of slavery.' To Washburne 13 Dec 1860 (pp.78-79): 'Let either be done, and immediately filibustering and extending slavery recommences. On that point hold firm, as with a chain of steel.' His own words are the conduct (a refusal to trade away restriction), not a self-assessment. The trait as opposition to extension, not abolition: the same letters keep the fugitive-slave clause enforced (Kellogg, p.78). STRONG.

Lincoln to Cameron 3 Jan 1861 (p.92): 'The more potent matter is wholly outside of Pennsylvania, and yet I am not at liberty to specify it' and 'No person living knows or has an intimation that I write this letter.' Bates diary 16 Dec 1860 (p.165): Lincoln 'did not state' who would fill the other departments, and 'assured me however, that I am the only man that he desired in the Cabinet, to whom he has yet spoken a [or] written a word'. Reserve kept in the conduct itself, dated before 5 Mar 1861, STRONG.

Lincoln to Chase 26 May 1860 (pp.20-21): glad 'of the indication that you stand ready', and a 'great consolation that so nearly all ... of those distinguished and able men are already in high position to do service'. To Chase 31 Dec 1860 (p.90): 'In these troublous times I would much like a conference with you. Please visit me here at once.' Lincoln wrote on 18 Dec 1860 that he had 'never yet seen Governor Chase' (to Raymond, p.84). A Republican opponent of his proposals gives him a name for good faith and patriotism, which supports high. Caution: the praise is for character, and the same speech doubts the remedy. Bates's diary of 1859 had quoted a newspaper that he was politically 'buried', so the reputation is dated to the secession winter.

Crittenden's joint resolution of 18 Dec 1860, read by the Secretary, Globe 36-2 p.114: Art. 2 'Congress shall have no power to abolish slavery in places under its exclusive jurisdiction, and situate within the limits of States that permit the holding of slaves', Art. 3 on the District of Columbia, Art. 4 'Congress shall have no power to prohibit or hinder the transportation of slaves from one State to another', and Art. 6 'no amendment shall be made to the Constitution which shall authorize or give to Congress any power to abolish or interfere with slavery in any of the States'. His own proposal is the conduct, STRONG, dated before 5 Mar 1861.

basis: Journal of the Missouri State Convention, July 1861 (first pagination): 31 July 1861 p.25 he is elected provisional Governor with 69 votes and 'Mr. Gamble having received a majority of all the votes cast, was declared elected', p.32 he 'having signified his readiness to take the oath of office' it was administered the same day. As Chairman of the committee he presented the Address to the People (p.27-28): 'We find high officers of the State Government engaged in actual hostilities with the forces of the United States, and blood has been shed upon the soil of Missouri', and 'The danger is imminent, and demands prompt and decisive measures of prevention.' In debate (second pagination p.73) he answered Wright on the Convention's power: 'It is a body assembled by the people ... in their original capacity.' Taking the governorship of a state whose elected Governor was in the field against the Union is the conduct, dated 31 July 1861, the last day the rule allows. STRONG as a record, but no man's words on his courage were found, so the support is by his act.

No contemporary leg dated before 5 Mar 1861 found. In the Journal and Proceedings of the Missouri State Convention, March 1861 (archive.org proceedings00knaprich), the only sittings before the boundary are 1 and 4 March: on 4 March Gamble moved that a Committee on Federal Relations of seven 'consider and report on the relations now existing between the Government of the United States, the Government and people of the different States, and the Government and people of this State' and that all propositions on those relations be referred to it, a procedural step that names no policy (Birch offered a substitute speaking of 'amicable restoration of the Federal Union'). Bates's diary 18 Feb 1861 (p.174) shows him on two Union tickets for the Convention ('Citizens' Union Ticket', 'Constitutional Union Ticket'), which is the tickets' stand, not his words. His report and speeches for compromise come on 9 to 21 March (the Convention's journal, e.g. 'Mr. Gamble, from the Committee on Federal Relations'), after the boundary, so they cannot count for a start value. His own hostile word for the abolition movement in the House is the conduct. The cell says opposes emancipation, and this goes to opposing abolition: no remark here of emancipation as such. Adams to Seward, No. 2, London 21 May 1861, printed in the Message of the President, 37th Cong. 2d sess. A minister only days in London putting the prospect of a break to the Foreign Secretary is the conduct. STRONG: his own despatch. The cell's old cite (Newton, 1913, ch.3) is retrospective and not a leg. Read at history.state.gov frus1861 d47 (the printing's page marks), not checked in the archive.org scan.

A senior officer of the day reporting that officers spoke of him 'with earnest admiration', dated before 5 Mar 1861, supports above. Senate roll calls of 16 Jan 1861, Globe 36-2 p.409: Trumbull voted yea on the motion to postpone Crittenden's resolutions to take up 'the bill (H. R. No. 23) for the admission of Kansas into the Union' (yeas 25, nays 30, lost) and yea on Clark's substitute, which struck out Crittenden's amendments and resolved that the Constitution 'needs to be obeyed rather than amended' and that relief lay not 'in new guarantees for particular interests, compromises for particular difficulties, or concessions to unreasonable demands' (yeas 25, nays 23, carried). Crittenden voted nay on both. Votes are conduct: STRONG that he stood against the slavery guarantees. Not a statement about slavery itself, so thin as a leg for the word antislavery. Lincoln's letter of 10 Dec 1860 to Trumbull asks him to hold the line on extension but is Lincoln's, not his.
